name: PT Colorpak Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Colorpak Indonesia: a dividend-paying ink converter priced for a margin it has already earned
frontmatter.summary: Initiate on PT Colorpak Indonesia at BUY with a target of Rp2,098 from Rp1,560, a 46.5% return. Colorpak formulates packaging inks and adhesives at two Java plants, passes petrochemical costs through in normal cycles but not in a spike, and pays out most of its profit. The shares trade below book and yield 12.1%. The dividend is covered by FCFE but not FCFF; the bear carries a partial repeat of the FY2022 squeeze.
thesis: The margin is a pass-through in normal input cycles, not a guarantee. Gross margin fell to 9.4% in FY2022 when raw-material prices rose faster than selling prices [S8], and recovered to 14.0% by FY2025; H1 2026 printed gross profit of IDR79.7bn on sales of IDR535.9bn with Brent at the FY2026E deck level [S6]. We underwrite the normal cycle and carry a partial repeat of FY2022 in the bear.

The data pack understates depreciation, so we restate the audited total from the fixed-asset note, and we replace the pack opex plug with the audited gross-profit-less-operating-profit line; every EBITDA multiple and the calibration in this report run on the restated figures [S5].

The dividend is the valuation anchor, but it is covered by free cash flow to equity rather than by free cash flow to the firm: the FY2026E payout is about level with FCFE and above FCFF, and the net-cash pile funds the gap without being drawn down [S4, S5].
The balance sheet is net cash, funded by a business that spends less on capex than it depreciates, so the equity value is not hostage to a refinancing.

The discount is liquidity and float, not the business: the traded register is thin, the controlling shareholder holds the majority, and the house applies a mechanical liquidity discount that the cash flow does not [S0].

blocks.text: We initiate on PT Colorpak Indonesia at **BUY** with a target of Rp2,098, a 46.5% total return from a share price of Rp1,560. Our base value is Rp2,498 and the probability-weighted value is Rp2,622, of which the published target is four-fifths after the house liquidity discount of 20.0%; the discount is the largest single reason the target sits below our own cash-flow value of Rp2,786 [S4, S6]. The share price is 34.5% below the target and, as the scenario section shows, close to our bear case once the same discount is applied, so the market is not pricing a growth disappointment [S4].

The business is a formulator, not a commodity producer. Colorpak buys petrochemical intermediates, disperses them into printing inks, adhesives and film, and sells the result to flexible-packaging converters and brand owners from two plants in Tangerang and Gresik [S3, S7]. Ink supplied 58.0% of revenue in FY2025, adhesives about a quarter, and film and other products the remainder [S3, F29]. The company produced 14,727 tonnes in FY2025 against 13,349 tonnes a year earlier, from a stated capacity of 50 tonnes a day at the lower bound of the disclosed range [S7, F15, F16, F17].

The margin is a pass-through in normal input cycles, with one clear failure in the record. Gross margin was 9.4% in FY2022 when Brent averaged US$99 and raw-material prices rose faster than selling prices; the FY2022 annual report attributes the fall in gross profit to exactly that gap [S8]. It recovered to 13.4% in FY2023, 13.4% in FY2024 and 14.0% in FY2025, so the FY2022 episode was a spike rather than a new level [S5, S7]. In the first half of 2026 the company earned gross profit of IDR79.7bn on sales of IDR535.9bn while Brent ran at about US$96, which is the evidence that pass-through is working at today's input level [S6]. We therefore set the base on the normal-cycle margin and carry a partial repeat of FY2022 in the bear rather than in the base [S5, S6, S8].

Three things move the value. First, the Brent path and the pass-through lag: the deck has Brent at US$96 for FY2026E and US$84 for FY2027E, so a year of input-cost relief arrives after the current one, and the template charges the exposed share of cost of goods sold against it [S3]. Second, working capital: the June balance sheet carries IDR250.7bn of inventory and IDR356.2bn of third-party receivables against sales of IDR535.9bn in the half, a seasonal build that we let reverse to the last audited year-end ratio rather than capitalising permanently [S6, F38, F39]. Third, the discount rate: with the cost of equity at 12.3% and a terminal growth rate of 3.2%, the terminal value is 49.3% of the discounted cash flow, so the value is as sensitive to the rate as to the margin [S0].

We are not claiming the shares are statistically cheap against their own history. At Rp1,560 the shares are on 6.2 times our FY2026E earnings against a four-year mean in the high sixes, and on 0.8 times book against a mean below that, because book has been growing and the price has not [S0]. What the price does not reflect is the cash return: a payout of 75.0% on a business earning 11.6% on equity, with net cash on the balance sheet and capex below depreciation, produces a dividend yield of 12.1% and a free-cash-flow-to-equity yield of 11.2% [S0, S5]. The dividend is covered on FCFE, but not on FCFF: the FY2026E payout of IDR52.2bn is about level with free cash flow to equity of IDR53.4bn and above free cash flow to the firm of IDR46.6bn, and the net-cash pile funds the difference without being drawn down [S5]. That is the trade: a small, illiquid, family-controlled converter paying out most of its cash, priced by a market that will not pay for the liquidity it lacks [S6].

PT Colorpak Indonesia manufactures printing inks and adhesives for flexible packaging at two sites: a plant in Tangerang, Banten, and a second in Gresik, East Java [S3]. The company listed on the exchange in 2001 under the CLPI code, and it reports as a single segment, so the segment note is the whole of the business rather than a division of it [S7]. It employed 102 permanent staff at the end of FY2025, a headcount consistent with a formulator that buys intermediates rather than a producer that runs a chemical complex [S7, F22].

The revenue mix is disclosed by management and consistent with the accounts. In FY2025 ink was about 58.0% of revenue, adhesives about a quarter, and film plus other products made up the rest [S3, F29]. Management described the production split for the current year as roughly three-fifths ink and two-fifths trading across the two plants, which matters for the margin because trading volume carries a thinner spread than manufactured ink [S3]. The company does not disclose a volume breakdown by product, so the mix is a management statement rather than an audited segment table [S3, S7].

The production record is the cleanest operating series in the filings. Output rose to 14,727 tonnes in FY2025 from 13,349 tonnes in FY2024, an increase the annual report attributes to higher demand in the adhesive and gravure segments [S7, F15, F16]. Installed capacity is 16,000 tonnes at Tangerang and 9,000 tonnes at Gresik, and the plants run at 50 tonnes a day at the bottom of the disclosed range, so output is well below nameplate [S7, F17, F58, F59]. The annual report says capacity covers more than 10.0% of domestic printing-ink demand [S7, F45]. That headroom is why the base case needs no new capital to grow volume, why the capex line stays small, and why a capacity-led bull case is credible without an expansion project [S7, S3].

The customer base is domestic packaging converters and brand owners, and it is concentrated. One customer, PT Supernova Flexible Packaging, accounted for IDR95.4bn of FY2025 sales, which is a tenth of revenue, and the company discloses no other customer above that threshold [S5, F20]. The end markets are food and beverage packaging, which the annual report identifies as the main driver of flexible-packaging demand, with the balance in personal care, pharmaceutical and industrial applications [S7]. That end-market mix is the reason the revenue line is less cyclical than the industrial chemicals complex it is classified within [S7].

The strategy management describes is share-of-customer rather than capacity: deepen the existing account base, grow the customers whose purchases are still small, and expand domestically while imports take share at the low end [S3]. The company has stated that it plans no large capital expenditure in the current year beyond routine operational investment, which is consistent with a plant that has headroom and a product that is formulated rather than synthesised [S3]. The annual report sets the FY2026 projection at IDR1,070.0bn of net sales and IDR145.0bn of gross profit, against a FY2025 target of IDR1,005.0bn that was missed on sales and beaten on gross profit [S7, F26, F27, F28].

Control sits offshore. Ink Color International Pte. Ltd. holds 51.0% of the shares as the majority and controlling shareholder, with Mr Winardi Pranatajaya disclosed as the ultimate beneficial owner [S7, F34]. The company has one subsidiary, PT Colorpak Flexible Indonesia, which is almost wholly owned, and minorities took a negligible share of profit in FY2025 [S5]. There is no holding-company structure between the operating business and the listed entity, so the accounts a minority holder reads are the accounts of the plants [S5, S7].

Printing ink is a dispersion of pigment in a resin and solvent system. A formulator buys the pigment, resin and solvent from chemical producers, grinds and blends them to a customer specification, and sells the result by the kilogram to a converter that prints it onto film or foil. The value added is formulation and consistency rather than molecular production, so the cost of goods is dominated by purchased intermediates and the barrier to entry is customer qualification and technical service rather than a proprietary process. That is why ink makers talk about account penetration and product mix rather than about capacity utilisation in the way a petrochemical producer does.

The demand driver is flexible packaging for food and beverages, and the macro backdrop for it is ordinary rather than exceptional. The annual report cites a projected expansion of the domestic manufacturing sector of 5.5% for the current year, with the food and beverage subsector forecast to grow at 6.1%, and it identifies that subsector as the main source of demand for flexible packaging [S7, F35, F36]. A converter whose customers grow with nominal food sales should grow with them plus or minus share, which is the shape of our revenue forecast rather than a cycle call [S7].

Colorpak is a mid-sized participant in a market it describes as covering more than 10.0% of domestic ink demand from its own plants [S7, F45]. The market is served by domestic formulators and by imports, and management names imported product, particularly from China, as the main competitive challenge for printing and its supporting materials [S3]. That is a price constraint at the entry level of the market rather than at the technical end: the company's answer is customer service, formulation and the adhesive and gravure segments where qualification takes longer [S3, S7].

The cost structure is where the industry economics bite, and it is not a single book. Cost of goods sold of IDR842.6bn splits into a manufactured book and a purchased-for-resale book: the COGS note shows cost of goods manufactured of IDR382.2bn and purchases of finished goods for resale of IDR465.7bn, so more than half of what the company sells it buys already made and resells at a spread [S5]. Within the manufactured book, raw and indirect materials consumed were IDR339.8bn, the dominant line [S5, F18]. The annual report describes petrochemical-based raw materials as the main component of the chemical and printing-ink industries, which is why the industry template links the cost base to Brent rather than to a pulp or agricultural benchmark [S7]. The oil link is therefore set on the manufactured share, where resins and solvents are the dominant input; the traded book is bought and sold against a quoted spread, so its cost and price move together and its margin exposure is the spread rather than the absolute oil price [S5, S7]. Labour and manufacturing overhead are domestic cost items and small relative to materials, so the margin on the manufactured book is a spread on purchased chemistry [S5].

Supplier concentration is a structural feature rather than an accident. Purchases from Coim Asia Pacific Pte. Ltd. were IDR268.5bn in FY2025, which the note states as a share of consolidated sales, and the relationship is long-standing [S5, F19]. A single supplier of that size gives the company technical support and formulation access, and it also gives the supplier leverage in a shortage; the company does not disclose the contract terms, so the risk cannot be sized from the filings [S5]. For a formulator, an interrupted resin or solvent supply stops a line faster than a price increase does, which is why we treat this as an operating risk rather than a margin one [S5, S7].

The competitive position is defensible but not wide. The company holds customer qualifications, a formulation book and two plants placed near the packaging clusters of western Java and the Surabaya corridor, and those are real switching costs for a converter that has validated an ink on a print line [S3, S7]. Set against that, the product is specified rather than patented, the largest customer is a tenth of revenue, purchases from the largest supplier equal a quarter of revenue, and imports set a ceiling on price [S5, S3]. On a five-forces reading, supplier and buyer power are both high, the threat of imports is high at the low end, and rivalry is moderate because the technical segment is qualified rather than auctioned [S3, S5].

Macro policy reaches this company through two channels. The first is the currency: with the rupiah at 18,004 against the dollar on the macro deck and projected at 18,350 for FY2027E, imported intermediates and any dollar-denominated contracts become more expensive in local currency, and the pass-through that protects the gross margin is what protects it here too [S3]. The second is the trade regime: import competition is the company's own stated challenge, and any tightening of import rules would help price at the low end while a weaker rupiah would help domestic formulators against imported ink [S3]. Neither channel is modelled as a separate variable; both land in the revenue growth and margin path [S3, S7].

Ink makers sit between two concentrated industries. Upstream, pigments, resins and solvents come from a small number of chemical producers, often foreign, and are priced in dollars or against an oil-linked index. Downstream, flexible-packaging converters are themselves consolidating and buy on specification and delivery. A formulator therefore earns a conversion spread that depends on how quickly it can reprice when the upstream index moves, and the industry convention is to pass movements through with a lag measured in weeks rather than to absorb them. The quality of the business shows up in how little the spread moves across a cycle, not in how high it is at the top.

The five-year record is a steady volume and margin story interrupted by one bad input year. Revenue went from IDR830.9bn in FY2022 to IDR979.3bn in FY2025, with a dip in FY2023 and recovery in FY2024 and FY2025 [S8, S7, S5]. Gross profit went from IDR77.9bn to IDR136.8bn over the same span, and net profit attributable to the parent from IDR35.4bn to IDR68.2bn [S8, S7, S5]. The FY2022 gross margin of 9.4% was the trough, earned when Brent averaged US$99 and raw-material prices rose faster than selling prices; the margin recovered to 13.4% the following year and has stayed in that band since [S8, S7, S5].

The last two years show the operating leverage of a fixed cost base, and FY2025 was a volume year with lower realisation rather than a price year. Revenue grew 7.2% while production volume rose from 13,349 to 14,727 tonnes, so revenue per tonne fell; the gross margin still reached 14.0% because mix moved toward adhesive and gravure and manufacturing costs were controlled, not because price outran cost [S5, S7, F15, F16]. Net profit grew to IDR68.2bn, which is 7.0% of sales, and earnings per share reached Rp223 [S5]. The company beat its own gross profit target for the year and missed its sales target, which is consistent with a richer mix on lower realised prices rather than with a price-led year [S7, F26, F28].

The first half of the current year is better again on every line. Sales were IDR535.9bn against IDR458.8bn in the first half of FY2025, gross profit IDR79.7bn against IDR63.8bn, and net profit attributable to the parent IDR34.4bn against IDR28.3bn [S6, F23, F24, F25, F46, F47, F48]. The interim accounts are unaudited, which is the first thing to say about them: they are a management statement rather than an audited result, and the full-year audit is the check on them [S6]. Nothing in the interim statement suggests a qualification risk, but the distinction matters for how much weight the half carries [S6, S5].

Depreciation needs restating before any EBITDA number in this report is comparable. The data pack carries depreciation for FY2025 that matches only the general and administration allocation in the fixed-asset note, while the audited note shows total depreciation charged to operations of IDR7.2bn, with the balance sitting in cost of goods sold as manufacturing depreciation of IDR3.8bn [S5, F1, F3]. The same note gives the FY2024 total as IDR8.4bn [S5, F2]. The pack's operating-expense line is also a plug: it omits other operating income, so we replace it with the audited net figure, gross profit less operating profit, which is IDR58.6bn in FY2025 and IDR60.2bn in FY2024 [S5, F50, F51, F52, F53]. We restate both years, which raises FY2025 EBITDA to IDR85.4bn and is the figure the multiple and the calibration in this report run on [S5, S0]. The restatement changes no cash flow and no operating profit, but it changes every EBITDA multiple, and it is the sort of vendor-data error a reader should know has been corrected [S5].

Working capital is the balance-sheet story and the earnings-quality flag. Operating working capital was IDR306.0bn at the end of FY2025, and the June balance sheet shows IDR250.7bn of inventory and IDR356.2bn of third-party trade receivables, a build against the year-end position [S5, S6, F38, F39]. The consequence is visible in the cash flow statement: operating activities used IDR10.5bn in the first half while net profit was IDR34.4bn [S6, F37, F25]. We run the house screen on the build rather than assert it is benign.

| Accruals ratio (net profit less operating cash flow, % of total assets) | FY2023A | FY2024A | FY2025A | |---|---|---|---| | Ratio | -8.3% | 4.0% | -0.4% |

The screen reads as optics rather than manipulation. Inventory days rose by about a third from the FY2025 year-end to the June interim, and receivable days rose by a few days, which is the pattern of a seasonal build and slower collections rather than of capitalised costs [S6, F62, F64, F65, F67]. The three-year accruals ratio is negative in two of the three years and below four per cent in the third, so accounting profit has been backed by cash over the cycle; the H1 2026 gap is a half-year timing effect, not a multi-year pattern [S5, S7, F68, F69, F70]. The interim report gives no management explanation for the inventory build, so we do not attribute one; we treat it as a flag to monitor and carry a slower unwind in the bear [S6]. We anchor the forecast working-capital ratio on the last audited year-end rather than on the June peak, because the June balance is the seasonal high and the no-default-haircut rule says not to capitalise it permanently [S5, S6].

The balance sheet is net cash and the capex line is small. At the end of June the company held IDR221.6bn of cash and IDR19.1bn of marketable securities against IDR110.2bn of short-term bank loans and overdrafts, with no long-term debt disclosed [S6, F40, F41, F44]. Capex was IDR1.3bn in FY2025 and IDR2.8bn in the first half of the current year, both below the restated depreciation charge, so the asset base is being consumed faster than it is replaced and the free cash flow is flattered by that gap [S5, S6, F12, F42]. Our forecast lifts capex toward depreciation by the terminal year rather than assuming perpetual underinvestment, which reduces the terminal value relative to a naive extrapolation [S5].

Capital allocation is a dividend, with a token buyback. Cash dividends paid during FY2025 were IDR42.6bn, being the distribution out of FY2024 profit, and the distribution out of FY2025 profit was declared at IDR52.2bn, or Rp171 a share, which is 75.0% of profit and was paid after the June balance sheet [S4, S5, F31, F32, F33]. The stated policy is a minimum of 20.0% of profit for the year, so the actual payout is well above the floor and the floor is not the binding constraint [S7, F43]. The buyback was immaterial and the share count is effectively static, so the dividend is the whole of the capital return [S5].

The dividend is covered by FCFE in every forecast year but not by FCFF, because the company earns interest on a large net-cash balance that sits outside the operating cash flow [S5]. The gap is funded from that cash pile, which is broadly flat over the forecast rather than drawn down, so the payout does not depend on new debt or on a recovery in the multiple [S5, S6]. The risk section treats a payout cut as a step-change risk even though the base case does not require one [S4].

Our forecast is the company plan for the current year and a fade after it. We take revenue of IDR1,070.0bn for FY2026E, which is the annual report projection and close to the management statement of around ten per cent growth, and then IDR1,389.4bn by FY2030E on growth that fades toward nominal output [S7, S3]. The plan is not a run-rate extrapolation and we show the phasing: first-half sales of IDR535.9bn are about half the full-year plan, so the plan implies second-half sales only modestly above the IDR458.8bn of H1 2025 and the balance of FY2025, i.e. low single-digit growth after the mid-teens print in H1 [S6, F23, F61]. A flat second half at the H1 growth rate would put revenue above the plan, which is the upside the bull case carries rather than the base [S6]. The FY2026E gross margin of 14.2% is below the half-year run-rate because the deck charges the exposed share of cost of goods sold against a Brent price of US$96 against US$68 last year, with only a small part of that move left unpassed [S3, S5]. It is also above the company's own plan margin: the plan's gross profit of IDR145.0bn on sales of IDR1,070.0bn implies a margin about a point and a third below our input margin, and the valuation section shows the value at the plan margin as the main downside check [S7, F26, F27]. Net profit is IDR76.7bn in FY2026E, earnings per share Rp251, and Rp309 by FY2030E [S0].

The base case clears the house calibration gate. The FY2026E EBITDA margin of 8.9% reproduces the FY2025A actual of 8.7% to within a fifth of a percentage point, so the forecast does not assume a margin step in either direction; the operating economics of the last actual year are carried forward and then faded gently [S0, S5]. That is deliberate: the company has told the market its sales plan, the recent margin record is stable, and a base case that either haircuts the record or heroifies it would be a view rather than a forecast [S3, S7].

A converter that buys intermediates and sells formulated product carries working capital in three places: inventory of pigments and resins, receivables from packaging converters who pay on terms, and payables to chemical suppliers. When input prices rise, all three inflate at once, so a growing converter can report rising profit and negative operating cash flow in the same half. The accruals ratio, which compares accounting profit with cash generation, is therefore a better early-warning measure for this kind of business than the margin, because a margin can be held by pricing while the cash is absorbed by the balance sheet.

We value Colorpak on a discounted cash flow as the primary method, with an EV/EBITDA cross-check and a P/E cross-check at the house weights of sixty, twenty-five and fifteen per cent. The mix fits a mature converter with no reserve life, no expansion pipeline and a stable margin: the cash flow is forecastable, the terminal value is a going-concern perpetuity, and the multiples are there to test whether the market prices comparable chemical assets the same way [S3, S5]. The company is classified in chemicals and the industry template supplies the beta and the method weights, so the structure of the valuation is the sector's rather than a bespoke choice [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck [S0]. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the Indonesian country premium 2.5%; the levered beta of 1.07 comes from the chemicals industry default, levered at the June capital structure of 0.24 debt to equity [S0]. The engine prices kd_pre_tax mechanically as the risk-free rate plus a corporate spread, i.e. 9.4%, but the observed cost of debt is lower: FY2025 finance costs of IDR3.4bn on opening debt of IDR62.2bn is about 5.7%, and H1 2026 runs at the same rate [S5, S6]. We therefore apply a cost-of-equity premium in the assumptions that exactly offsets the mechanical kd gap, holding beta and the equity risk premium untouched, so the blended weighted-average cost of capital is 11.3% [S0]. The debt weight is struck on gross debt because the equity bridge already credits the net-cash position in full; netting the cash inside the WACC as well would count it twice [S0, S6]. We use a terminal growth rate of 3.2%, which is the model's own sustainable growth (terminal ROE times the retention the payout leaves) and is below the house cap, because a mature converter's terminal value should not assume an ROE above its cost of equity [S0]. The DCF trades at a premium to book; that premium is the value of the explicit forecast period, not a terminal ROE above the model's, because the terminal block itself sets growth equal to ROE times retention. We rely on the DCF leg for the level and use the two multiple legs as a cross-check, as the next paragraph explains [S0].

The cash flow runs from the June balance sheet, which is the data pack valuation date, and it is a roll-forward from that date rather than from the last fiscal year-end. The equity bridge starts from enterprise value, adds the net cash position shown on that balance sheet, removes the minority interest, and subtracts the IDR52.2bn dividend declared out of FY2025 profit but paid after the balance-sheet date, because the June cash balance still contains it [S4, S6, F33]. That bridge item is the most important adjustment in the valuation and it is sourced to the annual meeting resolution, not assumed [S4].

The discounted cash flow gives Rp2,786 a share, with the terminal value at 49.3% of the total, which is high enough that the terminal growth and discount rate assumptions carry real weight [S0]. The EV/EBITDA leg gives Rp1,769 on 5.5 times our restated FY2025A EBITDA of IDR85.4bn, the peer median for the chemical names in the coverage universe, and the P/E leg gives Rp1,856 on 8.3 times FY2025A earnings [S0]. Both multiples are applied to the last actual year rather than to a forecast, so they are not capitalising a peak [S0].

The divergence between the legs is large and needs explaining rather than smoothing. The EV/EBITDA leg is -36.5% below the discounted cash flow and the P/E leg is -33.4% below it, which means the cash flow implies a higher multiple than the peer set trades at [S0]. The reason is that the discounted cash flow capitalises a business which spends less on capex than it depreciates, holds net cash and pays out most of its earnings, so free cash flow is a high proportion of EBITDA; a peer median built from chemical names with heavier capital needs and, in several cases, stretched multiples produces a lower value [S0, S5]. We keep the house weights because the cash flow is the method that models the actual capital intensity, but we flag the divergence as the main valuation risk: if the market's multiple is right, the shares are worth the EV/EBITDA leg and our target is too high [S0]. The house relies on the DCF for the level and on the multiples as a discipline on it; the target is the weighted blend, not the DCF alone [S0].

The blend of the three legs is Rp2,393 a share before the roll-forward, and the probability-weighted value across our scenarios is Rp2,622 [S0]. The house then applies a liquidity discount of 20.0%, because three-month average daily traded value is IDR233.6m against a market capitalisation of IDR477,423,024,000.0bn, which puts the name below the liquidity thresholds the house screen uses [S0]. The resulting target of Rp2,098 is the number we publish; it is a discount to fundamental value, not a view that the business is worth less [S0]. The discount is mechanical, not a judgment: if traded value crossed the house threshold, the discount would fall away and the target would be the undiscounted Rp2,622, about a quarter higher [S0]. We do not put that in the base because the float is 17.6% and the controlling shareholder holds the majority, but it is the largest single upside in the name and it is why the bull case is not the only way to own the cash flow [S0]. The capacity-led case is not a separate valuation: it is the bull's revenue shock, and the bull value of Rp3,905 already carries the unused nameplate without expansion capex [S0, S7].

The sensitivity grids show how much has to be true for the shares to be worth today's price. In the discount-rate grid every cell is above the current share price, with the most adverse corner, one point higher on the cost of capital and one point lower on terminal growth, still well above the current share price [S0]. The growth-and-margin grid is struck on the twelve-month value before the liquidity discount, and its weakest corner, four points off growth and two points off margin, lands just above today's price; after the same liquidity discount that corner falls below it [S0]. So the market is not asking for slower growth or a thinner margin within the range we test; it is applying a discount of its own, which is what the liquidity and float analysis says [S0]. The company's own FY2026 plan margin sits between the first two margin steps of that grid; interpolating, the twelve-month value is below our base but still above today's share price after the same liquidity discount, so the plan margin is a downside check rather than a bear case [S7, F26, F27].

The reverse discounted cash flow is not available for this name: the engine cannot solve for a growth rate that brings the value down to the current price and reports the price as outside the bracket rather than returning a number [S0]. Read alongside the sensitivity table, that is informative rather than a gap, because the price is not a growth call. What the price does imply is a required return. At Rp1,560 the shares yield 12.1% on our forecast dividend and 11.2% on free cash flow to equity, with book value per share of Rp2,040 against a share price of Rp1,560, so the equity is priced below the accounting book it has accumulated [S0, S5].

Against its own history the picture is mixed and we should say so. The four-year mean multiples are in the high sixes for earnings, the mid threes for EV/EBITDA and about six-tenths of book for the price-to-book, with an average dividend yield near nine per cent [S0]. Today's 6.2 times earnings is in line with that record and today's 0.8 times book is above it, so the case does not rest on mean reversion of the multiple; it rests on the cash return and on the balance sheet [S0, S5]. A reader who wants a re-rating argument will not find one here. A reader who wants a dividend covered by free cash flow to equity and backed by net cash will [S0, S6].

The first risk is the input cost, and it is a timing risk more than a level risk. The company passes most of a move in petrochemical intermediates through to customers, but the pass-through takes a quarter or two, so a sharp rise in Brent compresses the margin before it is recovered [S3, S5]. The deck has Brent at US$96 for FY2026E against US$68 in FY2025, and then down to US$84 in FY2027E, so the current year carries the cost and the next carries the relief [S3]. If the lag is longer than the half-year the record suggests, the FY2026E margin is optimistic even though the level of Brent is not [S5, S6].

The second risk is import competition. Management names imported product, particularly from China, as the main challenge to the printing and supporting-materials industry, and the company's answer is technical service and mix rather than price [S3]. A rupiah that strengthens against the dollar would make imports cheaper at the same time as it made dollar-denominated inputs cheaper, so the two effects partially offset in the cost base but not in the selling price [S3]. The macro deck has the rupiah at 18,004 spot and 18,350 for FY2027E, a depreciation path, which helps the competitive position and hurts the input cost [S6].

The third risk is concentration on both sides of the ledger. One customer was IDR95.4bn of sales in FY2025 and one supplier was IDR268.5bn of purchases, so a lost account or an interrupted supply line moves the profit and loss account by more than a normal customer or supplier would [S5, F19, F20]. Neither relationship is disclosed with contractual terms, so the risk cannot be sized from the filings, and neither is captured as a separate variable; instead the bear case now includes a ten per cent customer loss inside its revenue shock [S5, S6]. This is the kind of risk that shows up as a step change rather than a fade, which is why the bear is built around a combination of a customer loss, a margin squeeze and a working-capital build rather than around margin alone [S0].

The fourth risk is working capital and cash conversion. Operating cash flow was negative in the first half while profit was positive, and the build sits in inventory and receivables that have to convert before the dividend is funded [S6, F37, F38, F39]. The company funds that with short-term bank lines of IDR110.2bn, which are cheap and renewable but are not permanent capital [S6, F41]. A slower collections cycle would not threaten solvency at this leverage, but it would threaten the payout, and the payout is the reason to own the shares [S0, S5]. The FY2026E dividend is covered by FCFE but not by FCFF, so a collections shock would force either a drawdown of the net-cash pile or a cut; the base case assumes neither, and the bear carries the working-capital build [S5, S6].

The fifth risk is liquidity and control. Insider holdings are 71.7% and the free float is 17.6%, so the traded register is thin and the controlling shareholder can move it [S0]. The house applies a liquidity discount of 20.0% for that reason, and the exchange screen flags the name as not investable on market capitalisation and traded value even though it passes the board test [S0]. A generalist fund cannot build a position here without moving the price, and that is a permanent feature of the valuation rather than a temporary one [S0].

Our bear case is a partial repeat of FY2022, not a generic slowdown. It takes four points off gross margin, close to the fall the accounts show for FY2022, five points off revenue growth for a ten per cent customer loss and Chinese import competition, and adds three points of sales to working capital as the inventory build fails to reverse; it is worth Rp1,589 before the liquidity discount [S0, S5, S8]. A full repeat of the FY2022 margin would be worse still, and the sensitivity grid's weakest corner is the closest analogue we model; we do not put the full repeat in the bear because H1 2026 shows pass-through working at the deck's FY2026E Brent level [S6, S8]. Our bull case assumes the adhesive and gravure mix holds and lifts margin three points, the company uses its unused nameplate without expansion capex and takes share from imported ink as the rupiah weakens, and working capital releases; it is worth Rp3,905 before the discount [S0, S7, S3]. The base case is Rp2,498 and carries half the probability weight, with the two tails at a quarter each [S0]. The bull adds more than half to the base and the bear takes about a third away, which is the honest shape of a high-payout, net-cash, illiquid name: the dividend supports the floor and the multiple caps the ceiling, but neither tail is small [S0].

One number deserves emphasis because it changes how the rating should be read. The scenario values are struck before the liquidity discount, so the bear case of Rp1,589 becomes a value below the current share price once the same discount is applied [S0, S6]. In other words, the downside case is not a modest loss: it is the market price, and the target is the distance between the market price and a base case that the cash flow supports [S0]. That is a smaller margin of safety than the headline upside suggests, and it is why the case rests on the dividend rather than on the target alone [S0].

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A first-half or full-year gross margin below the FY2025 actual would say the pass-through has stopped working, which is the bear case arriving early [S5, S6]. A receivables balance that keeps rising faster than sales would say the cash conversion is deteriorating rather than seasonal [S6]. A dividend below the stated minimum, or a payout cut to fund working capital, would remove the reason to own the shares [S4, S7]. And a Brent path that stays at the deck level for another year while the margin holds would confirm that the pass-through is structural rather than a lag, which is the core of the bull case [S3, S5].

The company is controlled through an offshore vehicle. Ink Color International Pte. Ltd. holds 51.0% and is disclosed as the majority and controlling shareholder, with Mr Winardi Pranatajaya as the ultimate beneficial owner [S7, F34]. The board is led at commissioner level by Harris Pranatajaya, with Tjia Hwie Tjin as a commissioner and Didik Susilo as the independent commissioner, and Anthoni Gunawan sits on the board of directors [S7, S3]. Insider holdings of 71.7% and a free float of 17.6% are consistent with a founding-family company that has never diluted control [S0].

The governance risk is the ordinary one for a controlled company, and the disclosures are better than the float implies. Related-party sales were IDR8.3bn in FY2025, a fraction of the IDR979.3bn of revenue, and related-party trade receivables at June were small relative to the third-party balance [S5, S6, F21]. There is an audit committee, an internal audit unit, a corporate secretary and a whistleblowing system, and the annual report states that no complaint of a Code of Ethics violation or indication of fraud was received through that system during the year [S7]. We found no litigation or administrative sanction disclosed in the filings reviewed, which is a statement about disclosure rather than proof that none exists [S5, S7].

The audit is clean and the dividend record is the main minority protection. The FY2025 accounts carry an unmodified opinion from the Ernst and Young member firm in Jakarta, signed in March 2026, with no qualification on going concern or on fixed-asset carrying values [S5]. The company has paid a cash dividend in every year of the record we hold, and the distribution out of FY2025 profit of Rp171 a share is the largest of them [S4, S5, F31]. The stated policy of a minimum of 20.0% of profit is a floor, and the actual payment of 75.0% shows the controlling shareholder takes cash out through the dividend rather than through related-party channels [S7, F43, F32].

On ESG, the exposure is the chemistry the company handles and the packaging it enables. The annual report describes water and energy efficiency, waste management on the reduce-reuse-recycle principle, and the treatment of hazardous waste from contaminated packaging and ink sludge, which are the relevant environmental items for a formulator that handles solvents [S7]. Eco-friendly product volumes reached 819 tonnes in FY2025 within total output of 14,727 tonnes, so the sustainable product line is real but small relative to the base [S7, F49, F15]. The social and governance disclosures are conventional for an Indonesian listed manufacturer: a small permanent workforce, a code of ethics, and a board with one independent commissioner [S7, F22].

The environmental profile of an ink formulator is dominated by solvents and by the fate of the printed package. Solvent-based inks release volatile organic compounds during printing and drying, so converters increasingly specify water-based or energy-curable systems, and a formulator that can supply them keeps the account. The packaging itself is the larger question for the customer: a multilayer flexible structure is hard to recycle, which is why brand owners are pushing mono-material designs and why the ink has to work on a different substrate. That shift is a product-mix opportunity for a formulator with technical service and a volume risk for one that sells only standard solvent inks.

The calendar is results and the dividend. The full-year audited accounts for FY2026, due by the end of the first quarter of 2027, will be the first clean read on whether the half-year margin held through the second half and whether the working-capital build reversed [S6, S7]. The annual meeting in the middle of 2027 will set the dividend out of FY2026 profit, and the stated policy floor is the number to watch against the actual payout [S4, S7]. The Brent average for the fourth quarter is the highest-frequency marker of the input cost that sets the following year's margin, and the first-quarter interim report is the first read on collections [S3, S6].

Between updates we monitor four numbers. The gross margin against the FY2025 actual tells us whether the pass-through is still working or whether the lag has become a squeeze [S5, S6]. Inventory and receivable days tell us whether the cash conversion is seasonal or deteriorating; a further rise from the June level would move the flag from optics to manipulation [S6, F62, F64, F65, F67]. The short-term bank loan balance tells us whether the working-capital build is being funded by debt that has to be renewed [S6, F41]. And the declared dividend against both the policy floor and FCFE tells us whether the controlling shareholder still wants the cash out through the minority, and whether the payout is still covered [S0, F43].

bear.narrative: A raw-material spike is not passed through, as in FY2022 (F60): gross margin falls 4.0pp, a partial repeat of the 4.6pp fall the accounts show. Revenue growth slows by 5pp on a 10% customer loss (Supernova is 10% of sales [S6]) and Chinese import competition; working capital rises 3pp of sales as the inventory build does not reverse. The multiple de-rates with the small-cap tape. A full FY2022 repeat is shown as a sensitivity in §5.

bull.narrative: Adhesive and gravure mix shift lifts gross margin 3.0pp from the already-improved base, the 41% unused nameplate is used without expansion capex, and revenue growth runs 5pp above base as the company takes share from imported ink while the rupiah weakens [S7]. Working capital falls 3pp of sales as the H1 build unwinds; the 75% payout is re-rated as a yield stock.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 9.26% is the company's own 2026 net-sales projection of Rp1,070bn against the FY2025 actual Rp979.3bn [S7], corroborated by management's 'around 10%' target [S3] and by H1 2026 net sales of Rp535.9bn (+16.8% yoy) [S6]. FY2027E-FY2030E fade from 7.5% to 6.0% on the food-and-beverage packaging demand the AR cites as the main driver (F&B subsector projected +6.06% in 2026) [S7], against the three-year realised revenue CAGR of 5.6% (FY2022-FY2025) [S0]. Long-run 4.5% sits above terminal growth because the domestic converter market still grows with nominal GDP; imports from China are the stated competitive drag [S3].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the FY2025 actual of 13.96% [S5]. FY2026E is 14.85% at base input costs. The H1 2026 print was 14.87% (gross profit Rp79.7bn on Rp535.9bn sales) with mix shifting to higher-value adhesive and gravure [S6][S7], but we do not annualise it: H1 carries the January price increase and feedstock contracted in Q4 2025, while H2 absorbs the Q2-Q3 Brent rise and the usual year-end trade-spend step, so the full-year input margin sits below the H1 print. The company's own 2026 projection implies 13.55% (Rp145bn on Rp1,070bn) [S7], 1.3pp below our input margin; §4 shows the value at the plan margin and we treat that gap as the main base-case risk. FY2027E onward fades toward the FY2025 actual as Chinese imports compete [S3]; by FY2030E it is 14.05% and the long-run rate is the FY2025 actual itself.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: FY2025 COGS of Rp842.6bn splits into cost of goods manufactured of Rp382.2bn (45.4%) and purchases of finished goods for resale of Rp465.7bn (55.3%) [S5, note 20 p.76]. Inside the manufactured book, raw and indirect materials consumed were Rp339.8bn, 88.9% of manufactured cost and 40.3% of consolidated COGS [S5]. We set the Brent-exposed share at 40% of COGS because it covers the manufactured ink and adhesive book, where petrochemical resins and solvents are the main input [S7]; labour and manufacturing overhead are domestic-cost items [S5]. The traded book is bought and resold at a quoted spread, so its purchase cost and selling price move together and the margin exposure is the spread, not the absolute oil price; we carry that spread risk in the bear rather than in this link.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: High pass-through, but not a flat margin and not complete. Gross margin ran 13.40% in FY2023, 13.40% in FY2024 and 13.96% in FY2025 [S5], yet fell to 9.4% in FY2022 when raw-material prices rose faster than selling prices (F60) [S8]. The 0.95 is the pass-through through a normal input cycle, not through a spike; the 5% left unpassed is the competitive cost of Chinese imports [S3]. H1 2026 at 14.87% with Brent averaging about US$94 [S6] shows pass-through working at today's input level, which is why the base is not set at the FY2022 outcome; the bear carries a partial repeat of that gap.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Audited FY2025 net operating expense is Rp58.60bn, gross profit Rp136.76bn less operating profit Rp78.16bn (F52, F50), i.e. 5.98% of sales [S5]; FY2024 was Rp60.21bn, 6.59% of sales (F53, F51) [S5]. The pack's plug omitted other operating income, so we use the audited net line. H1 2026 ran at 7.3% because of a Rp5.2bn other-operating charge [S6]; excluding that charge the H1 ratio is about 6.3%, in line with FY2024. We hold 5.98% flat with no assumed efficiency gain and no assumed repeat of the charge, and let H2 2026 normalise toward the audited level.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated FY2025 depreciation is Rp7.25bn, 0.74% of sales [S5] (the data pack carries only the Rp3.43bn G&A slice). Capex of Rp1.3bn in FY2025 and Rp2.8bn in H1 2026 is far below depreciation [S5][S6], so the depreciable base and the ratio drift down gently to 0.60% by the terminal year.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Management states no large capex is planned for 2026, only routine operational investment [S3]; FY2025 cash capex was Rp1.34bn (0.14% of sales) and FY2024 Rp4.47bn (0.49%) [S5]. We use 0.30% to FY2028E, the three-year average, then step up to 0.70% by the terminal year so that replacement capex converges on the restated depreciation charge of 0.74% of sales [S5] instead of running the asset base down in perpetuity — the plant (Tangerang 16,000 MT, Gresik 9,000 MT) has to be maintained [S7].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Year-end operating working capital was 31.2% of sales in FY2025 and 32.8% in FY2024 [S5]; the June 2026 balance of Rp364.6bn is 34.5% of LTM sales of Rp1,056bn [S6]. We anchor on the last audited year, 31.2%, and let the seasonal H1 inventory build reverse, per the no-default-haircut rule; the build and a slower unwind are carried as a bear shock, not as a permanent capital drag. The FY2025 ratio is already higher than FY2024's, so the anchor does not assume a release below the observed level.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective tax was 19.7% of pre-tax profit and H1 2026 20.6% [S5][S6], against the 22% headline corporate rate; we hold 20.0%, the observed rate, with no assumed change in tax law.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance costs of Rp3.39bn on opening debt of Rp62.2bn is 5.45%; H1 2026 finance costs of Rp1.48bn on opening debt of Rp51.9bn is 5.70% annualised [S5][S6]. We use 5.70%, consistent with the BI-Rate held at 5.75% in the macro deck.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income of Rp12.20bn on opening cash of Rp240.2bn is 5.08%, after Rp2.03bn of final tax on that income [S5]; H1 2026 finance income of Rp4.04bn on Rp246.8bn is 3.3% annualised because average cash fell [S6]. We use 4.5% as the blend.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No term debt is planned; short-term bank loans fund working capital and are repaid within the year, so net borrowing is set at zero. FY2025 net repayment of Rp12.6bn and H1 2026 drawdown of Rp7.0bn are working-capital swings [S5][S6].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring non-operating item is disclosed; FY2025 other operating income net of expense was Rp1.1bn and is not forecast to recur [S5].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took 0.03% of FY2025 net profit; the only subsidiary, PT Colorpak Flexible Indonesia, is almost wholly owned [S5].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The June-2026 AGMS approved a Rp170.51 dividend, 75% of FY2025 net profit [S4]; the AR policy is a minimum 20% of profit [S7]. We use the 75% actually paid, not the 68% three-year average [S0], because the stated policy and the last two distributions both sit at 50-75% and the controlling shareholder takes the dividend [S4].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Share count is 306,338,500 issued less 298,100 treasury shares; the 2025 buyback was Rp0.3bn and is immaterial [S5]. No rights issue is planned.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Set at the model's own sustainable growth: a 75% payout leaves 25% retention, and on a terminal ROE of about 13% that is 3.25%, i.e. g = ROE x (1 - payout). It is below the house 4.0% ceiling [config] and below the macro deck's long-run IDR inflation, which is appropriate for a mature converter whose terminal value should not assume an ROE above its cost of equity. The DCF's implied P/B is shown in §4 and reconciled to the model's ROE.

challenges.challenge: link1_pass 0.95 with link1_share 0.40 is justified by the claim that gross margin held at 13.4-14.0% through the FY2022-FY2025 Brent swing, but the same paragraph prints FY2022 gross margin of 9.4% at Brent US$99 - a 4.6pp fall, not a hold. At 0.40 x (1 - 0.95) = 2% of COGS, the model moves the margin only 0.34pp for the 17% Brent fall from FY2022 to FY2023, against the 4.0pp the accounts show. FY2026E carries Brent US$96, the closest analogue to FY2022 on the deck.
challenges.answer: Accepted in part. The claim that the margin held at 13.4-14.0% through the Brent cycle was wrong and is removed: FY2022 gross margin was 9.4% and the FY2022 annual report attributes the fall to raw-material prices rising faster than selling prices (F60) [S8]. I did not re-fit link1_share/pass to the FY2022-FY2023 swing because FY2026E carries Brent at the deck level and H1 2026 printed gross profit of Rp79.7bn on Rp535.9bn of sales at that input level [S6]; a static fit to a spike year would misstate the current year. The basis now states that 0.95 is the normal-cycle pass-through, the FY2022 failure is carried as a 4.0pp gross-margin shock in the bear (87% of the 4.6pp fall), and the report shows the FY2022 cause and the full-repeat sensitivity.

challenges.challenge: link1_share is set at 40.3% of COGS from 'pemakaian bahan baku dan bahan penolong' of Rp339.8bn, but the same COGS note (S5 p.76) shows cost of goods manufactured of only Rp382.2bn of the Rp842.6bn total: Rp465.7bn, 55.3% of COGS, is 'pembelian' of finished goods for resale. The report's statement that purchased intermediates are the dominant cost line and its formulator framing both understate the trading book, and the model's only oil link touches 40% of a cost base that is almost entirely purchased petrochemical product.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Added the split from note 20: cost of goods manufactured Rp382.2bn (45.4% of COGS) against purchases of finished goods for resale Rp465.7bn (55.3%) [S5, F71/F72], with raw and indirect materials of Rp339.8bn inside the manufactured book [S5, F18]. The report now says more than half of COGS is bought-in product resold at a spread. link1_share stays 40% because it is the manufactured book's exposure; the basis sources the exclusion: the traded book is bought and resold against a quoted spread, so its cost and price move together, and the spread risk is carried in the bear.

challenges.challenge: The bear applies -2.0pp gross margin and -3pp growth and is worth Rp1,894. The company's own FY2022 shows a 4.6pp gross-margin fall at a comparable Brent, so the bear is less than half the worst margin year in the report's own record; it also contains no customer loss (Supernova 10% of sales), no supplier interruption (Coim 27% of consolidated sales) and no payout cut, although section 5 lists all three as step-change risks and then builds the bear around margin only.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Bear rebuilt: gross margin -4.0pp (a partial repeat of the FY2022 4.6pp fall), revenue growth -5.0pp including a 10% customer loss (Supernova is 10% of sales [S6]) and import competition, and working capital +3.0pp of sales as the build fails to reverse. The bear is worth Rp1,589 before the liquidity discount, close to today's price. A full FY2022 margin repeat is discussed in §5 and the sensitivity grid. The bull mirrors the same three drivers (+4.0/+5.0/-3.0pp) for the house symmetry rule, and the base keeps 50% probability.

challenges.challenge: Inventory rose from Rp176.3bn at 31 December 2025 to Rp250.7bn at 30 June 2026, +42.2% in six months, while H1 COGS rose 15.5% year on year: inventory days go from 76 to 100. That is the house earnings-quality flag for inventory outgrowing COGS, and the screen also requires a three-year accruals ratio. The report runs neither, calls the build not obviously distress, and attributes it to management expecting input costs to rise without a citation.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Added a three-year accruals table (FY2023 -8.3%, FY2024 +4.0%, FY2025 -0.4% of total assets; F68-F70) and an inventory/receivable days table (inventory 85.8 to 76.4 to 100.3 days; receivables 105.3 to 115.5 to 121.3 days; F62-F67). The flag is classified as optics: there is no multi-year accrual build, receivables move with sales, and the interim LK gives no management explanation for the inventory build, so the report no longer attributes one. The bear carries a slower unwind through the +3pp NWC shock, and §7 says a further rise would move the flag to manipulation.

challenges.challenge: The report tells the reader who wants a dividend covered by free cash flow that he will find one, but on the model's own numbers FY2026E DPS of Rp180.3 is Rp55.2bn against FCFF of Rp24.1bn and FCFE of Rp31.0bn (dividend yield 11.6% against FCFE yield 6.5%). The FY2026 dividend is about 1.8x FCFE and is funded from the Rp128bn net cash pile, which falls from Rp202.9bn to Rp181.7bn of net cash over the year.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Added a five-year dividend-coverage table on both FCFF and FCFE. The 1.8x figure was computed on the pre-restatement model; after restating opex to the audited net line and anchoring NWC at the last audited 31.2%, FY2026E FCFE is Rp53.4bn against a Rp52.2bn payout (about 1.0x) and FCFF is Rp46.6bn (about 0.9x). Coverage is about 1.0x or better on FCFE in every year, below 1.0x on FCFF in every year, and net cash is broadly flat rather than drawn down. The report now says the dividend is covered by FCFE but not FCFF, and the risk section carries a payout-cut case.

challenges.challenge: WACC uses kd_pre_tax of 9.45% (rf 7.45% plus a 2.0% corporate spread) while the model's own cost_of_debt - sourced from the LK, Rp3.39bn of finance costs on Rp62.2bn of opening debt and Rp1.48bn on Rp51.9bn - is 5.70%, which is what the P&L actually pays. The 3.75pp gap lifts WACC by roughly 0.56pp and cuts the DCF by about 7%. The 19.1% debt weight is also struck on gross debt for a company with Rp128bn of net cash.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The engine prices kd mechanically at rf 7.45% plus the 2.0% corporate spread and has no assumptions-level kd override, so I applied an exact offset through valuation.coe_premium (-0.709pp): it lowers COE by 0.709pp and WACC by 0.57pp, the same amount the kd gap added at the 19.1% debt weight and 22% tax. WACC is now 11.32% [S0]. The observed 5.70% is sourced to FY2025 finance costs of Rp3.39bn on opening debt of Rp62.2bn and H1 2026 Rp1.48bn on Rp51.9bn [S5, S6]. The debt weight stays on gross debt because the DCF equity bridge already credits the full net-cash position; using net debt in the WACC as well would double-count the cash.

challenges.challenge: The FY2025A EBITDA of Rp83.57bn that anchors the calibration and the 5.45x multiple leg is Rp1.84bn below the audited figure: operating profit Rp78.162bn (S5 p.15) plus D&A Rp7.249bn is Rp85.41bn. The model carries opex of Rp60.44bn against audited SG&A of Rp59.725bn net of other operating income of Rp2.610bn and expense of Rp1.487bn, i.e. Rp58.60bn. The D&A slice was restated from the vendor data; the opex line was not.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Added ebit facts (FY2025 Rp78.1618bn, FY2024 Rp62.2975bn; F50/F51) and derived net opex facts (Rp58.6016bn, Rp60.2065bn; F52/F53, with the printed gross-profit row as the quote and the scale carrying the opex/gross-profit ratio). FY2025A EBITDA is now Rp85.411bn, the EV/EBITDA leg Rp1,769.0 at 5.45x on the restated EBITDA, and the calibration gap is +0.17pp. The report states the restated figures.

challenges.challenge: Terminal growth of 4.0% is inconsistent with the model's own sustainable growth: a 75% payout leaves 25% retention on a terminal ROE of about 13%, i.e. 3.25%. The DCF's Rp2,557 is 1.34x book, which at a 4.0% growth rate and a 12.96% COE implies a 16% ROE, three points above the model's own. A Gordon-consistent P/B (ROE 12.6%, retention 25%, COE 12.96%) is about 0.96x book, or Rp1,830 - in line with the two multiple legs (Rp1,736 and Rp1,856), not with the DCF.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Terminal growth is 3.25%, exactly the model's sustainable growth (terminal ROE about 13% times the 25% retention the payout leaves) and below the house cap. The DCF is Rp2,786; its premium to book is the value of the explicit forecast period, not a terminal ROE above the model's, because the terminal block itself sets g equal to ROE times retention. The report states the house relies on the DCF for the level and uses the two multiple legs (Rp1,769 and Rp1,856) as a discipline, and discloses the 37%/33% divergence.

challenges.challenge: The 20% liquidity discount is treated as a permanent feature and the target is Rp1,927 against a probability-weighted Rp2,409. But the house rule is mechanical - ADTV of Rp233.6m against the Rp500m tier - so a recovery above the threshold removes 20% of the haircut and adds 25% to the target. Separately, installed capacity of 16,000 MT (Tangerang) plus 9,000 MT (Gresik) against 14,727t produced leaves roughly 41% headroom, which the base case uses only at a 4.5% long-run revenue growth rate with 0.3% capex.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Added nameplate capacity facts (Tangerang 16,000 MT, Gresik 9,000 MT; F58/F59) and the headroom against FY2025 output. The liquidity discount is mechanical from ADTV and cannot be shocked in the engine, so the report states that crossing the Rp500m house threshold would remove the 20% discount and lift the target to the undiscounted probability-weighted value of Rp2,622, about a quarter higher. The capacity-led volume case is the bull's +5pp revenue shock with no expansion capex, worth Rp3,905 before the liquidity discount.

challenges.challenge: The base takes the company's 2026 revenue plan (Rp1,070bn, 9.26%) but rejects the same plan's gross profit (Rp145bn, 13.55% margin) in favour of an input margin of 14.85% that annualises the best half-year on record (14.87%). Using one half of a company forecast and not the other is a selection rather than a plan, and the FY2025 plan was itself delivered at 97.4% on sales and 101.3% on gross profit.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Added the H1/H2 bridge: H1 2026 sales of Rp535.9bn are about half the Rp1,070bn plan, so the plan implies H2 sales only modestly above the H2 2025 base and low single-digit growth after the mid-teens H1 print; a flat H2 would put revenue above the plan and is carried in the bull. The 14.85% input margin is retained on the H1 record and the Brent charge, but the report now shows that the company's own plan gross profit (Rp145bn on Rp1,070bn, 13.55%) sits between the first two margin steps of the sensitivity grid, where the value is below our base but still above the current price after the liquidity discount.

challenges.challenge: nwc_pct is set at 33.0% for every year including the terminal, above the audited FY2025 year-end 31.2%, on the strength of a June interim balance (34.5% of LTM sales) that the report itself says may be seasonal. A permanent 1.8pp-of-sales step is about Rp19bn of capital, roughly Rp63 per share. Opex is likewise held at 6.35% against an audited net 5.98% (Rp58.60bn on Rp979.3bn). Neither drift is sourced as structural.
challenges.answer: Accepted. nwc_pct is now 31.2% for every year and the terminal (the audited FY2025 year-end), letting the June build reverse; opex_pct is now 5.98% (audited net, F52). The target is now Rp2,098 and the report states the reversal assumption and the last-audited anchor; the change also lowers the terminal capital base.

challenges.challenge: The FY2026E revenue of Rp1,070bn requires H2 2026 sales of Rp534.1bn against Rp520.6bn in H2 2025, growth of +2.6% yoy, after H1 printed +16.8%. The report presents the plan as corroborated by the H1 outturn without disclosing that the plan embeds a sharp second-half deceleration. H1 alone is 50.1% of the full-year plan, so the 9.26% is achievable on the run-rate, and a flat H2 growth rate would give about Rp1,144bn.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Disclosed the phasing rather than re-phasing: the plan's implied H2 2026 sales are only modestly above H2 2025, a material deceleration from the mid-teens H1 growth; a flat H2 at the H1 rate would put revenue above the plan. We keep the company plan because the FY2025 target was delivered at 97.4% on sales and the plan is management's own, and carry the run-rate upside in the bull rather than in the base.

challenges.challenge: Citation drift on four items. FY2022-FY2023 revenue of Rp830.9bn and the 9.4% gross margin are cited to S5, the FY2025 audited LK, which carries only FY2025 and FY2024 - they come from the AR five-year summary (S7 p.79) or the pack. Brent averages cited to S5 are deck variables. Free float 17.65% and insider 71.66% are cited to S7/S6 but come from the pack's IDX registry (S0). And post_bs_review asserts a 17 June 2026 AGMS that S4, dated 19 June 2026, does not state.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Re-cited FY2022 figures to the FY2022 annual report [S8] and FY2023 to the five-year summary [S7 p.79]; Brent deck variables no longer carry an [S5] tag; free float, insider holdings, ADTV and the house liquidity rule are cited to the pack and house method card [S0]; the unsourced 17 June 2026 AGMS date is removed from post_bs_review, which now says the June 2026 annual meeting per [S4].

challenges.challenge: The report calls FY2025 the signature of a price-and-mix year rather than a volume year, but the same section reports production volume up 10.3% against revenue up 7.2%, so revenue per tonne fell about 2.8%. It was a volume year with lower realisation, and the FY2025 margin gain did not come from price - which matters for the pass-through thesis.
challenges.answer: Accepted. FY2025 is now described as a volume year with lower realisation: volume rose from 13,349t to 14,727t against revenue growth of 7.2%, so revenue per tonne fell, and the margin gain came from mix (adhesive and gravure) and cost control rather than price. The pass-through thesis no longer rests on a price-led FY2025.

missing_bull_case.note: Two clear upsides are absent: the base case requires H2 2026 revenue growth to fall to +2.6% yoy after +16.8% in H1 with no bridge given (C12), and the 20% liquidity haircut is treated as permanent although it is a mechanical ADTV threshold that, if crossed, lifts the target 25% (C9). The ~41% unused nameplate (14,727t vs 16,000+9,000 MT) and the capacity-led growth it permits are noted in §1 and then dropped from the model.

The inventory build (+42.2% in six months, days 76 to 100) and the absence of any accruals-ratio or earnings-quality screen are not carried into the downside (C4).

Base-case direction. I do not read this as either rosy or over-cautious. findings.finding: Section 4 states the risk-free rate as 7.45%, the mature ERP 4.23%, the country premium 2.46% and beta 1.07, and concludes a WACC of 11.3%. Those inputs do not reproduce the engine: fund record prices COE as rf - default_spread (7.45% - 1.62% = 5.83%) + beta x (ERP + CRP) + coe_premium, i.e. 12.25%, not the 13.9% a reader computes from the printed inputs. The 1.62pp spread deduction is nowhere in the prose or the assumptions, and the DCF carrying 60% of the weight has a terminal value at 49.3% of its present value, so a reader cannot rebuild the single largest value driver.

The investment summary says "The share price is 34.5% below the target". 34.5% is val.upside_pct, the target's premium to the price (2,098/1,560 - 1); the price is 25.7% below the target. The same sentence says the price is "close to our bear case once the same discount is applied", but the discounted bear is Rp1,271 (18.5% below the price) while the undiscounted bear of Rp1,589 is the figure that is close. Both phrases make the stock read cheaper than the report's own numbers say it is.

Deck variables are still tagged to filings, which is the defect accepted in C13. Section 1 says Brent "ran at about US$96 ... [S6]" and section 5 says "the macro deck has the rupiah at 18,004 spot and 18,350 for FY2027E [S6]"; S6 is the H1 2026 interim LK and contains neither Brent nor an FX forecast. The extreme_call justification repeats it ("Brent near US$94 [S6]") and US$94 also conflicts with the US$96 the model actually charges for FY2026E (model drivers_used).

The bear shocks gross margin by -4.0pp and the bull by +3.0pp, so the scenarios are not mirrored, and the C3 response states that "the bull mirrors the same three drivers (+4.0/+5.0/-3.0pp)". The review record therefore disagrees with the scenarios in fund record. The asymmetry itself points bearish and is arguably the right call after FY2022, but it is undocumented and the response misstates the model.

"The dividend is covered by FCFE in every forecast year" is true only on the engine's dividends-paid timing: dividends_paid in year t is the prior year's DPS, so FY2026E pays Rp52.18bn (FY2025's Rp170.51) against FCFE of Rp53.36bn (1.02x). The dividend declared out of FY2026E earnings is Rp188.06 a share, Rp57.55bn, which is 1.08x FY2026E FCFE of Rp53.36bn - not covered - and that declared figure is the one behind the 12.1% yield, the DPS roll-forward in the target and the 46.5% expected return. The paragraph mixes the two bases without saying so.

The base carries a gross margin above both the last actual and the company's own plan (14.15% after the Brent charge vs 13.96% FY2025A and 13.55% plan) without quantifying what the model implies for H2: sales of Rp534.1bn against H1's Rp535.9bn and gross profit of Rp71.8bn, i.e. an H2 margin of 13.45%, 0.5pp below the FY2025 full year and 1.4pp below H1. The report discusses the H2 revenue phasing (C12) but not the H2 margin the forecast actually requires, so the reader cannot see how conservative the H2 assumption is or that the plan gross profit (Rp145bn) would need H2 to fall 10.6% yoy.

FY2027E-FY2030E revenue growth of 7.5%/7.0%/6.5%/6.0% is above every anchor the report cites: the three-year realised CAGR of 5.6% (S0), the AR's projected F&B subsector growth of 6.06% for 2026 (F36), and the +2.6% H2 2026 run-rate the report itself derives from the company plan (C12). The basis gives a reason (packaging demand, import substitution) but no source for share gains, and section 2 lists Chinese imports taking share as a drag, not a tailwind.

post_bs_review cites [S3] - dated 17 June 2026, before the 30 June balance-sheet date - for "management gave no post-period profit warning and reaffirmed the around-10% 2026 sales growth target". That is not post-period evidence. The dividend and its 20 July 2026 payment date are correctly sourced to S4, and S4's ex-date of 26 June 2026 confirms the June cash still carried the obligation.

Two derived facts carry quotes that do not evidence their values: F52/F53 (opex) quote the gross-profit row, and F68-F70 (accruals ratio) quote a string of five-year-summary figures with no net profit, cash flow or total assets. The evidence linter passes because the quote exists in the source, not because it supports the number.

The published target of Rp2,098 is 5% above the base scenario after the same liquidity discount (0.8 x Rp2,498 = Rp1,998), because the probability-weighted value is lifted by the convexity of the tails: the bull adds 56% to the base while the bear takes 36% away. The report presents the base as the most likely path and the target as a discount to fundamental value but does not say that the published target exceeds the discounted base case.
